sources.title: Standard deviations and standard errors
sources.version: BMJ 2005;331(7521):903, Statistics Notes series; full text as archived in PubMed Central, retrieved 2026-07-25. DOI 10.1136/bmj.331.7521.903, PMID 16223828, PMCID PMC1255808
sources.locator: Whole article: the contrast between the standard deviation as a measure of variability and the standard error as the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean; the relation SE = SD divided by the square root of the sample size; the behaviour of each as the sample grows; and the closing passage on unlabelled plus-or-minus notation
sources.license: Copyright 2005, BMJ Publishing Group Ltd; free full text made available through PubMed Central. No open reuse licence is stated, so this pack uses the article for facts only.

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts it states: that a sample standard deviation describes variability among observed individuals while a standard error describes uncertainty around an estimated mean; that sample means vary across samples and the standard deviation of their sampling distribution is the standard error; that the estimated standard error is obtained by dividing the sample standard deviation by the square root of the sample size; that this estimate falls as sample size increases; that about 95% of values in a normal distribution lie within two standard deviations of the mean; that the sampling-distribution principle extends to proportions, regression coefficients, and contrasts such as a difference between two means; and that a review of 88 articles published in 2002 found 12 (14%) failed to identify which measure of dispersion was reported, after which the BMJ adopted a policy of removing plus-or-minus signs and asking authors to state which quantity is quoted. No sentence, table, figure, or example from the article is reproduced or adapted. The cohort, every worked figure, and all wording in this lesson are original.

sources.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, section 1.3.6.6.1: Normal Distribution
creators: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology, U.S. Department of Commerce
sources.version: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, online edition retrieved 2026-07-25; no publication or revision date is stated on the page
sources.locator: Section 1.3.6.6.1, Normal Distribution, under the heading 'Theroretical Justification - Central Limit Theorem'
sources.license: US Government work; NIST states that information on its sites is public information and may be distributed or copied, with credit requested

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the bounded central-limit result that, for independent observations from one finite-variance population, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normality as sample size grows, is centred at the population mean, and has spread governed by the population standard deviation divided by the square root of sample size. No wording, table, figure, or example from the handbook is reproduced or adapted; the theorem statement in the lesson was independently synthesized and every illustration around it is original. NIST copyright guidance at https://www.nist.gov/oism/copyrights states that NIST information is public information that may be distributed or copied and requests appropriate credit.

sources.title: Central limit theorem: the cornerstone of modern statistics
sources.version: Korean Journal of Anesthesiology 2017;70(2):144-156; full text as archived in PubMed Central, retrieved 2026-07-25. DOI 10.4097/kjae.2017.70.2.144, PMID 28367284, PMCID PMC5370305
sources.locator: Sections on sampling distributions of small populations, the statement of the central limit theorem, and the discussion showing how population shape and sample size affect the sampling distribution of a mean
sources.license: Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial License (CC BY-NC 4.0), as stated on the article page

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts that a skewed population does not prevent sample means from approaching normality as sample size increases under the theorem's conditions, that the means are centred at the population mean with variance equal to the population variance divided by sample size, and that population shape and sample size affect the finite-sample approximation. The article's size-30 discussion is not used as a general central-limit threshold. No wording, table, figure, worked demonstration, or example from the article is reproduced or adapted, and the article's non-commercial licence condition is not relied on because nothing from it is reused. The decision order, pharmacy example, and every other illustration in this lesson are original.
